hmmt-feb-2000-calc-01.title: Second derivative
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-01.body:
$y'=3x^2-6x+6$, $y''=6x-6$, which vanishes at $x=1$ (and changes sign there). The slope at $x=1$ is $y'(1)=3-6+6=3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-02.title: Maximise the net gain per pull
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-02.body:
Each pull gives a net gain of $g(x)=x-x^3$ feet. $g'(x)=1-3x^2=0$ gives $x=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ (the positive root), and $g''<0$ there, so this is the maximum net gain per pull: $\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}$ ft.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$ feet**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-03.title: Signed area must vanish
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-03.body:
The rectangle is $0\le x\le\frac\pi4$, $-2\le y\le2$, symmetric about the x-axis. The curve (which stays inside the rectangle) splits the area in half exactly when the area above equals the area below, i.e. when the signed area between the curve and the x-axis is zero:
$$\int_0^{\pi/4}(\sin x+C)\,dx=\left[-\cos x+Cx\right]_0^{\pi/4}=1-\frac{\sqrt2}2+\frac{\pi}{4}C=0.$$
So $C=-\frac4\pi\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)=\frac{2\sqrt2-4}{\pi}\approx-0.373$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt2-4}{\pi}$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-04.title: AM-GM
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-04.body:
For $0<x<\frac\pi2$, $\tan x>0$ and $\tan x\cdot\cot x=1$, so $\tan x+\cot x\ge2$ with equality iff $\tan x=\cot x=1$, i.e. $x=\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi4$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-04.title: Calculus
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-04.body:
With $y=\tan x>0$ we minimise $y+\frac1y$; the derivative $1-\frac1{y^2}$ vanishes at $y=1$ and the function decreases before and increases after. So $\tan x=1$, $x=\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi4$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-05.title: Differentiate the series
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-05.body:
For $|x|<1$ the series may be differentiated term by term: $f'(x)=\sum_{i\ge1}x^{i-1}=\frac1{1-x}$. Also $f(0)=0$. Integrating, $f(x)=-\ln(1-x)$.

**Answer: $f(x)=-\ln(1-x)$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-06.title: Minimise the length of a segment touching the inner corner
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-06.body:
Put the outer corner at the origin with the hallways along the positive axes, so the inner corner is $(6,6\sqrt5)$. A pipe touching the inner corner with one end $(x_0,0)$ on one wall, $x_0>6$, has its other end on the other wall at height $y_1=\frac{6\sqrt5\,x_0}{x_0-6}$, so its length squared is $L^2=x_0^2+\frac{180x_0^2}{(x_0-6)^2}$. The longest pipe that fits is the minimum of $L$ over $x_0$.

$\frac{d}{dx_0}L^2=2x_0-\frac{2160\,x_0}{(x_0-6)^3}=0\Rightarrow(x_0-6)^3=1080=216\cdot5\Rightarrow x_0-6=6\sqrt[3]5$.

With $c=\sqrt[3]5$: $x_0=6(1+c)$ and $L^2=36(1+c)^2+\frac{180(1+c)^2}{c^2}=36(1+c)^2\left(1+\frac{5}{c^2}\right)=36(1+c)^2(1+c)=36(1+c)^3$, since $5=c^3$.

So $L=6(1+\sqrt[3]5)^{3/2}\approx26.8$ feet.

**Answer: $6\left(1+\sqrt[3]5\right)^{3/2}\approx26.77$ ft**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-06.title: Known formula
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-06.body:
The classical result for hallways of widths $w_1,w_2$ is $L=\left(w_1^{2/3}+w_2^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}$. With $w_1=6$, $w_2=6\sqrt5$: $w_2^{2/3}=6^{2/3}5^{1/3}$, so $L=6\left(1+5^{1/3}\right)^{3/2}$.

**Answer: $6\left(1+\sqrt[3]5\right)^{3/2}$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-07.title: Eliminate the parameter
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-07.body:
Let $F(x,x_0)=\frac2{x_0}+x-\frac{x}{x_0^2}$. The envelope consists of points where the line touches the curve, which satisfy $F=y$ and $\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_0}=0$: $-\frac2{x_0^2}+\frac{2x}{x_0^3}=0$, so $x_0=x$. Substituting, $y=\frac2x+x-\frac1x=x+\frac1x$ for $x>0$.

Check: the curve $y=x+\frac1x$ has tangent at $x=x_0$: $y=x_0+\frac1{x_0}+\left(1-\frac1{x_0^2}\right)(x-x_0)=\frac2{x_0}+x\left(1-\frac1{x_0^2}\right)$, which is exactly the given line.

**Answer: $y=x+\frac1x$ for $x>0$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-08.title: Symmetry trick
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-08.body:
Let $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\sin\theta\,d\theta$. The substitution $\theta\to\frac\pi2-\theta$ shows $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\cos\theta\,d\theta$. Adding, $2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin\theta\cos\theta)\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(\ln\sin2\theta-\ln2\right)d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\sin2\theta\,d\theta-\frac\pi2\ln2$. With $\alpha=2\theta$, $\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\sin2\theta\,d\theta=\frac12\int_0^{\pi}\ln\sin\alpha\,d\alpha=I$ (by symmetry about $\frac\pi2$). So $2I=I-\frac\pi2\ln2$, $I=-\frac\pi2\ln2$.

**Answer: $-\frac\pi2\ln2$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-09.title: Self-similarity
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-09.body:
The pattern repeats after two radicals: $f=\sqrt{x+\sqrt{0+f}}=\sqrt{x+\sqrt f}$, so $(f^2-x)^2=f$. If $f(a)=4$ then $(16-a)^2=4$, and since $f^2-x=\sqrt f>0$ we need $16-a=2$, $a=14$.

Differentiate $(f^2-x)^2=f$: $2(f^2-x)(2ff'-1)=f'$. At $f=4$, $x=14$: $4(8f'-1)=f'$, so $31f'=4$, $f'=\frac4{31}$.

**Answer: $\frac4{31}$**

hmmt-feb-2000-calc-10.title: Follow the ray
hmmt-feb-2000-calc-10.body:
The ray $y=x-9$ passes through the opening at $x=9$. Reflect at the flat walls $y=\pm1$ (slope flips sign): it hits $(8,-1)$, $(6,1)$, $(4,-1)$, $(2,1)$ (4 bounces), then continues along $y=x-1$ and meets the parabola $x=y^2$ at $\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2},\frac{1-\sqrt5}2\right)\approx(0.382,-0.618)$ (bounce 5).

The tangent to the lower branch $y=-\sqrt x$ there has slope $-\frac1{2\sqrt x}\approx-0.81$. Reflecting the direction $(1,1)$ in this tangent line gives the direction $\approx(0.769,1.187)$, i.e. slope $\approx1.54$.

After that the ray bounces between the walls, advancing $2/1.54\approx1.30$ in $x$ per bounce: at $x\approx1.43,2.73,4.02,5.32,6.62,7.91$ (bounces 6 to 11). The next wall hit would be at $x\approx9.21>9$, which is beyond the end of the mirror, so the ray leaves.

Total bounces: $4+1+6=11$.

**Answer: 11**
